Metabolic rates in the Trinidadian guppy from the LP Oropuche stream (Poecilia reticulata LPO) were measured under controlled laboratory conditions to establish baseline energetic demands. Using closed-system respirometry on juveniles with a mean wet body mass of approximately 74 milligrams, the rate of oxygen consumption was determined to be 0.0176 milligrams per hour  when measured at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This measurement provides a crucial reference point for understanding the basal maintenance requirements of this population. The relatively small body size of these fish, even as juveniles, dictates a high mass-specific metabolic rate, a pattern commonly observed across small-bodied poeciliids. The precise quantification of this metabolic trait allows for more accurate comparisons with other guppy populations inhabiting different predation regimes along the Caroni drainage system, where variations in flow and canopy cover may impose distinct energetic constraints.

Growth trajectories for the LP Oropuche strain of Poecilia reticulata LPO were analysed to estimate the maximum attainable body size under near-optimal feeding conditions. The laboratory diet, designed to support approximately 90 percent of the growth achievable with unlimited food, allowed the fish to approach a mean maximum standard length at the F1 generation. Applying a correction factor of ten-ninths to this observed F1 mean maximum length provides an estimate of the ultimate standard length, which was calculated to be approximately 3.51 centimeters [Li = approximately 3.51 centimeters]. This value represents the theoretical asymptotic length for individuals in this population when constraints on food availability are effectively removed. Such an estimate is valuable for parameterising comparative life-history models and highlights the prodigious growth potential inherent in this lineage, which contrasts sharply with the stunted sizes often observed in guppies from high-predation environments where resource allocation is heavily skewed toward early reproduction.

Variation in maternal provisioning was examined by comparing the mean dry weights of neonates born to females reared under contrasting dietary regimes from birth. Offspring produced by mothers maintained on a consistently high food ration exhibited a mean dry weight at birth of 0.00138 grams , reflecting a substantial investment of maternal resources into each individual offspring. In contrast, neonates born to mothers subjected to a restricted, low food diet during their development had a slightly higher mean dry weight of 0.00145 grams . This counterintuitive result, where food-limited mothers produced marginally heavier offspring, suggests a strategic shift in resource allocation. Under nutritional stress, females may concentrate their limited energetic budget into producing fewer but larger neonates, thereby enhancing the competitive ability and starvation resistance of each offspring during the critical early stages of exogenous feeding in the variable stream environment.

The mean interval between successive parturitions was calculated from the first four reproductive events of females maintained under high food conditions at a constant water temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This analysis yielded a mean age at birth of 29.03 days [ab = 29.03 days] for females on the high food ration, indicating a relatively rapid reproductive cycle under favourable nutritional circumstances at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. The consistent thermal environment eliminates temperature-driven variation in gestation length, allowing the direct effect of food availability on brood interval to be isolated. This rapid turnover of generations is a hallmark of the opportunistic life-history strategy adopted by guppies in productive habitats, enabling swift population growth. Under these high-resource conditions, the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and gestation are met efficiently, minimising the delay between successive broods and maximising the intrinsic rate of population increase.

When the same inter-parturition analysis was applied to females reared on a restricted low food diet at the identical temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], a discernible lengthening of the reproductive cycle was observed. The mean age at birth for these resource-limited individuals was recorded as 30.18 days [ab = 30.18 days], which represents a modest but biologically significant delay compared to their high-food counterparts at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This approximately one-day extension of the brood interval reflects the physiological challenge of allocating scarce energy towards both somatic maintenance and reproductive tissue synthesis. The ability to maintain regular parturition, albeit at a slightly slower pace, demonstrates a remarkable resilience to nutritional stress. Interestingly, this deceleration occurs despite the concurrent production of heavier neonates, suggesting a trade-off where the timing of reproduction is slightly prolonged to allow for the enhanced per-offspring investment observed in the low-food treatment group.
